title: Dysbiosis modulates CD8 + tissue-resident memory cells through a mechanism requiring polyamine metabolism during HIV infection

sections.abstract: Polyamines play crucial roles in modulating T lymphocyte functions. Here, we demonstrate that the oral mucosa of people living with HIV (PLWH), characterized by active polyamine metabolic pathways, exhibits significantly diminished IFN-γ expression and reduced abundance of CD8 + tissue-resident memory (T RM ) cells. Salivary 16S rRNA sequencing revealed elevated levels of Fusobacteria, negatively correlating with the levels of CD8 + T RM -like cells in PLWH. In vitro experiments showed that Fusobacterium nucleatum (FN) produced putrescine, which is known to be enriched in PLWH mucosa. Polyamines, HIV infection, and FN led to EIF-5A hypusination, diminished IFN-γ expression in CD8 + T cells, which impaired the proliferation of TRM-like cells in tonsil organoid cells. The inhibition of polyamine synthesis and EIF-5A hypusination restored IFN-γ expression and T RM -like cells. Collectively, these results highlight an essential role of polyamines in the critical interplay between oral resident microbiota, immunometabolic regulation, and immune competence during chronic viral infections.
sections.introduction: Mucosal immunity in people living with HIV (PLWH) has been a major focus of research, as mucosal surfaces are key sites of immune dysfunction during chronic infections. While combined antiretroviral therapy (cART) effectively suppresses viremia and partially restores peripheral CD4 + T cell counts, incomplete recovery of mucosal immunity, likely due to persistent immune activation and disruptions in the microbiota, is the Achilles heel in PLWH. Although HIV-specific resident memory CD8 + T cells are studied in peripheral blood and are enriched in human lymphoid tissues of HIV-elite controllers, 1 , 2 mucosal CD8 memory compartments are largely unexplored in PLWH. CD8 T RM are a subset of memory T cells characterized by their ability to persist long-term and rapidly respond to antigen re-exposure in tissues, and their functions are regulated by CD4 + T cells and cytokines. 3 Depending on the type of tissue, chronic viral infections can maintain, expand T RM populations, or cause their functional exhaustion in affected tissues due to ongoing antigen exposure. Although the oral mucosa of PLWH exhibits CD4 + T cell hyperactivation and FOXP3+ regulatory T cell (T reg ) dysfunction, 4 , 5 the fate of CD8 + T cells and their functions have not been evaluated previously. Polyamine metabolism is a critical biological process that has been recently demonstrated to determine the functional fates of CD4 + T cells. 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 Arginine-polyamine metabolism is also implicated in CD8 memory T cell responses. 10 , 11 However, the role of polyamines in adaptive immunity in mucosal tissue environments that function in the milieu of tightly-regulated interactions between immune cells and microbiome is limited. 9 Here, our study reveals how the polyamine pathway is impacted by HIV infection and how it controls T cell memory in oral mucosal tissues. Our results revealed that HIV and oral dysbiosis impair CD8 T RM cell proliferation by repressing IFN-γ in an EIF5A signaling-dependent manner. These findings underscore a compelling connection between HIV infection, dysbiosis, and excessive polyamine synthesis in contributing to T cell dysfunction during chronic mucosal inflammation.

Human gingival biopsies and saliva were obtained with informed consents from healthy control (Control; n=32) and HIV+ (PLWH; n=46) participants under a University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center Institutional Review Board-approved protocol. 4 , 5 The characteristics of enrolled participants for obtaining gingival biopsies and saliva are described in Table S1 , in the same cohort as in our previous stsudies. 4 , 5 Only a subset of gingival and saliva samples was available for paired correlation analysis described here. Discarded palatine tonsils were obtained from tonsillectomies at University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center via the Histology Tissue Procurement Facility, under a separate IRB-exempt protocol. Gingival biopsies were processed fresh for flow cytometry, while fresh or cryopreserved tonsil cells were analyzed by flow cytometry or used to establish HTOC cultures. Single-cell suspensions of gingival and tonsil tissues were prepared by digestion with Collagenase 1A (0.5 mg/mL; Sigma C9891), followed by Ficoll-Paque PLUS (GE17-1440-02; Millipore Sigma) centrifugation at 900 g and PBS washes. Cryopreserved, sterilely collected whole saliva samples were used for metabolomics and 16S rRNA sequencing.

HTOC cultures were setup by resuspending collagenase-digested tonsillar cells at 1 million/well cell density in regular or transwell culture plates. 4 , 54 They were TCR-stimulated with α-CD3 (1 μg/ml) and α-CD28 (1 μg/ml) antibodies, TGF-β1 (10 ng/ml) and IL-2 (100 U/ml) for 24- 36 hours before infection in multiple replicate wells. 4 , 55 Cells were cultured in complete RPMI-1640 (Hyclone) containing 10% human serum, 100 U/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, 2 mM glutamine, 25 mM HEPES, and 1 mM sodium pyruvate. In some experiments, putrescine dihydrochloride (100 μM), spermidine (0.1-1mM), and inhibitors were added at culture initiation. For HIV infection, replication-competent HIV X4-tropic NL43-GFP-IRES-Nef or HIV-NLGNef (∼1.7 ng), a recombinant NL4-3-based virus expressing GFP and Nef on a bicistronic transcript, was used. Cells plated in 200 μL volumes were spinoculated. 4 , 44 , 45 Confirmatory experiments were performed using both X4- and R5-tropic viruses. 45 The R5-tropic virus was generated by replacing the Env region in NL43-GFP-IRES-Nef with the CCR5-tropic HIV-1 ADA envelope from NLAD8 (NIH AIDS Reagent Program). 44 , 46 After 24–36 h post-infection, Efavirenz (50 nM; SML1284-1ML, Millipore Sigma), FN lysate, IFN-γ (20 ng/mL; RC217-17, BioBasic), anti-IFN-γ (10 μg/mL; NIB42, 16-7318-81, Invitrogen), and relevant inhibitors (DFMO, GC7) were added to cultures. Cells were then expanded for 4–7 days before flow cytometry and other assays. TCR-stimulating antibodies for CD3 (HIT3a, BD Biosciences) and CD28 (CD28.2, Thermo Fisher Scientific) were used in culture. Recombinant TGF-β1 was sourced from R&D Systems and BioLegend, while recombinant IL-2 was from BioBasic (Amherst, NY). DFMO, GC7, putrescine dihydrochloride, and spermidine were from Millipore Sigma.

Primary antibodies for surface and intracellular staining were used at 1:50–1:200 dilutions (or per manufacturer’s instructions). Flow cytometry secondary antibodies (anti-rabbit PE for hypusine staining) were from Jackson ImmunoResearch or Invitrogen/Thermo Fisher Scientific and used at 1:500–1:800 dilutions. Proper controls (unstimulated, unstained, isotype, secondary alone, single stain, FMO) were included for gate determination. PBMCs served as additional tissue controls. Cultures were restimulated with PMA (50 ng/mL) and ionomycin (500 ng/mL) for 4 h, with brefeldin A (10 μg/mL) added during the final 2 h, before intracellular cytokine staining. Data were acquired on BD Fortessa cytometers (BD FACSDiva v7) and analyzed with FlowJo (v9.8–10.7.1). CD8 + T cell populations were gated on lymphocyte, singlet, viable, CD3 + , and CD8 + or CD4− populations, as detailed in figure legends.

Fusobacterium nucleatum subsp. nucleatum ATCC 25586 was grown under anaerobic conditions at 37°C for 18 h in different broth media in glass test tubes in triplicates. 26 , 56 Undefined media included Tryptic Soy broth (Fisher Scientific) supplemented 0.5% yeast extract (Sigma) and 1% peptone (Thomas Scientific) (TSBYEP) with or without 10 mM ornithine. Defined media included oral chemically defined media containing 20 mM D-glucose and 10 mM D-sucrose with 1M 3-(N-morpholino) propane sulfonic acid and prepared without polyamines, with or without 10 mM ornithine. 25 After cultures were grown, supernatants and lysates were prepared as follows. All cultures were centrifuged at 4000 x g for 10 min to separate supernatants from cell pellets. Supernatants were passed through a 0.2 μm filter to remove any cellular debris. The cell pellets were washed twice in 1x phosphate-buffered saline (pH 7.4) and resuspended in extraction buffer (50 mM Trizma base, 0.1 mM EDTA, and 1 mM 2-mercaptoethanol [pH 7.5]). Cells were then mechanically lysed with 0.1 mm zirconium beads for 30 seconds three times using the Bead Ruptor 24 (Omni International, Inc). Cell lysates were centrifuged at 4 C° at 16,000 x g for 2 min. Supernatants of lysed cells were passed through a 0.2 μm filter to remove any remaining cell debris or un-lysed cells. Media controls without FN growth were included for comparison. 26 Supernatants and lysates were stored at -20 C° until LC-MS analysis or cell culture usage.

Bacterial DNA Isolation : Bacterial DNA was extracted from 50 uL of saliva per sample using QIAamp PowerFecal Pro DNA Kit (Qiagen) and following the provided manufacturer protocol. ZymoBIOMICS™ Microbial Community Standard (Zymo Research Corporation) and UltraPure™ DNase/RNase-Free Distilled Water (Invitrogen) were used as positive and negative controls respectively and were processed in parallel with the samples. 16S rRNA sequencing : PCR amplification was performed using primers that targeted the V4 region of the 16S gene: 5’- GTG CCA GCM GCC GCG GTA A-3’ for the forward primer and 5’- GGA CTA CHV GGG TWT CTA AT-3’ for the reverse primer. The PCR reaction was done in a reaction well plate using 5 ul template DNA, 2.5 ul Gold Buffer (10X), 2.5 ul MgCl2 (25 mM), 0.5 dNTP (10 mM), 1 ul each of the forward and reverse primers (10 uM), 0.25 ul AmpliTaq Gold DNA Polymerase (5 U/ul), and 12.25 ul UltraPure DNase/RNase-free distilled water (Invitrogen). The PCR amplification conditions were set to the following settings: 95C for 3 minutes, then 28 cycles of 95C for 30 seconds, 55C for 30 seconds, and 72C for 30 seconds, then finishing at 72C for 5 minutes. Amplicons were then purified using Ampure XP Beads and confirmed with the TapeStation 4150 (Agilent). DNA was quantified using Quant-iT™ dsDNA Assay Kits HS (Invitrogen) and normalized to 4 nM. The pooled library was diluted to 8 pM with 10% spike-in of 12.5 pM PhiX before running on the Illumina MiSeq, using 500 cycles v2 PE reagents, yielding 2 x 250 bp paired-end reads (Illumina). 16S rRNA data processing : Sequence reads were analyzed for quality control with the DADA2 pipeline (version 1.26). Pair-end reads for each sample were assembled into contigs and primer sequences were trimmed. Sequences were classified using the Ribosomal Database Project (RDP) taxonomy database (version 16). Taxa that were detected at higher average levels in the negative water controls relative to the samples were removed as contaminants. OTUs were assigned based on their most specific taxa hits prior to downstream analysis. OTUs were categorized as “undistinguishable” if the database is unable to classify the sequence beyond domain or class. Low abundance taxa were binned to “other” if it accounted for < 0.025% of total species detected across all samples. Quality control : Sequence quality control and denoising were performed using QIIME 2 (v2024.5), 49 an open-source bioinformatics pipeline for microbiome analysis. Low-quality bases (quality score < 30) at the sequence ends were trimmed, and sequences shorter than 100 nucleotides were excluded. The DADA2 48 plugin was applied to filter and correct sequencing errors, infer amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), and remove chimeric sequences. Specifically, the first 15 bases of both forward and reverse reads were trimmed to remove primers and low-quality regions, while forward and reverse reads were truncated at 240 bp and 220 bp, respectively to retain high-quality regions. This procedure ensured the removal of sequencing errors while preserving high-resolution ASVs for downstream taxonomic and diversity analyses. Taxonomy assignment : To minimize sequencing noise and consolidate similar sequences, de novo operational taxonomic unit (OTU) clustering was performed using VSEARCH within QIIME 2. Sequences were clustered at 99% sequence identity, grouping highly similar sequences into the same OTU. For bacterial microbiome analysis, filtered amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were taxonomically classified using the QIIME 2 feature-classifier plugin, which applies a naïve Bayes classifier trained on the SILVA reference database. 57 SILVA is a widely recognized, high-quality ribosomal RNA (rRNA) reference database that enables accurate taxonomic annotation of microbial communities. 52 Taxonomic assignment was performed using the pre-trained naïve Bayes classifier based on SILVA release 138, with a 99% sequence identity threshold. The resulting OTU tables and taxonomy assignments were integrated into two phyloseq objects 58 in .RData format for downstream statistical and visualization analyses. The phyloseq framework facilitates streamlined microbiome data management, supporting efficient implementation of alpha diversity, beta diversity, and differential abundance analyses. Alpha Diversity Analysis : Alpha diversity was assessed using two metrics: the Shannon index and the Chao1 richness estimator. The Shannon index incorporates both species richness and evenness, providing a measure of diversity within each sample, while the Chao1 index estimates species richness, particularly accounting for rare taxa. These metrics were computed for each sample using R (v4.4.1) vegan package, and differences in alpha diversity were evaluated between the two groups. Statistical significance was assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric method suitable for comparing distributions between two independent groups. Multiple testing corrections were applied where appropriate to control for false discovery rates. Beta Diversity Analysis: Beta diversity was assessed to compare microbial community composition across samples using the weighted UniFrac distance metric, 59 a phylogenetic-based measure that accounts for both taxonomic relatedness and relative abundance. The weighted UniFrac distances were computed using the GUniFrac package in R. To evaluate differences in microbial community composition between HIV+ and HIV− groups, permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) was performed on pairwise weighted UniFrac distances using the adonis2 function from the ape package in R, with 999 permutations. To visualize the beta diversity patterns, principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was conducted on the weighted UniFrac distance matrix using the cmd scale function from the R base package. The first two principal coordinate axes were plotted to capture the major sources of variation in microbial community structure across samples. Differential Abundance Analysis : To identify microbial taxa that significantly differed between the two groups, differential abundance analysis was conducted using the Linear Discriminant Analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) method. 60 LEfSe is a statistical approach designed to detect biologically meaningful differences in microbiome composition by integrating non-parametric statistical tests with Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). LEfSe analysis was performed using the microbiome Marker package in R. For microbiome data, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (for two-group comparisons) and the Kruskal-Wallis test (for multi-group comparisons) were applied with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. The LDA score cutoff was set to 2.0 to ensure the selection of strongly discriminative microbial features. To control for multiple testing, p-values were adjusted using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. To visualize the hierarchical structure of microbial biomarkers identified by LEfSe, a taxonomy tree was constructed using the BAZE package. This representation facilitates the interpretation of taxonomic relationships among differentially abundant microbial taxa. For the key microbial markers identified through LEfSe analysis, we further examined their association with Control and PLWH groups using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. To ensure robust statistical inference, p-values were adjusted using both FDR correction and Bonferroni adjustment, minimizing the risk of false-positive findings. This stringent approach enhances the reliability of conclusions regarding the significance of microbial differences between the groups in comparison.

Sample preparation, sequencing, alignment, and analyses were performed by Novogene. Strand-specific libraries were generated using the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq2500 (TruSeq V4 chemistry) with a paired-end 150 bp protocol (PE150). Raw reads (125 bp paired-end FASTQ files) were trimmed with Trimmomatic v0.30 to remove adapters and aligned to the human genome using STAR v2.5 with the GENCODE v4 (Ensembl 78) annotation. Gene counts from gingival biopsies (three biological replicates) were normalized with limma v3.26.8 and analyzed by unpaired t -test. Normalized counts were converted to RPKM values for heatmap visualization.

Sample collection: Human saliva samples were collected in 50 mL sterile tubes and stored at −80 °C. 4 , 5 For LC-MS analysis (Creative Proteomics), 100 μL frozen aliquots were thawed, transferred to new tubes, and extracted with 200 μL of 80% methanol. Samples were vortexed (30 s), incubated at −40 °C for 1 h, vortexed again (30 s), and centrifuged (10,000 g, 4 °C, 15 min). 200 μL of supernatant and 5 μL of internal standard (DL-o-Chlorophenylalanine, 1 mg/mL) were transferred to vials. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by pooling equal amounts of extracts from all samples and processed identically.

Instrumental setup: Analysis was performed on an Ultimate 3000LC coupled to a Q Exactive MS (Thermo) using ESI-MS in targeted MS/MS mode. Chromatographic separation was achieved with an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm) at 40 °C and a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (0.05% formic acid in water) and solvent B (acetonitrile) with a gradient: 0–1.0 min, 95% A; 1.0–12.0 min, 95%–5% A; 12.0–13.5 min, 5% A; 13.5–13.6 min, 5%–95% A; 13.6–16 min, 95% A. The sample manager was maintained at 4 °C.

ESI+: Heater Temp 300 °C; Sheath Gas 45 arb; Aux Gas 15 arb; Sweep Gas 1 arb; Spray Voltage 3.0 kV; Capillary Temp 350 °C; S-Lens RF 30%.

ESI−: Heater Temp 300 °C; Sheath Gas 45 arb; Aux Gas 15 arb; Sweep Gas 1 arb; Spray Voltage 3.2 kV; Capillary Temp 350 °C; S-Lens RF 60%.

Bioinformatics analysis: Data analysis included multivariate and single-variable analyses, clustering, and correlation network construction of differential metabolites. Metabolite identifications were made using Compound Discoverer 3.1 SP1 and MZmine2 softwares in our previous study. 5 MS1 and MS2 spectra were matched using a mass tolerance of m/z = 0.1.

Serially diluted standard solutions of the five polyamines were prepared in 10% acetonitrile. Cell lysates and supernatants from three independent experiments were processed and analyzed separately. For derivatization, 40 μL of each thawed supernatant or standard solution was mixed with 80 μL of 20 mM dansyl chloride solution and 20 μL of borate buffer and incubated at 40 °C for 30 minutes. UPLC-MRM/MS analysis was performed at Creative Proteomics: 10 μL of each derivatized sample was injected onto a C18 column (2.1 × 150 mm, 1.8 μm) and separated on an Agilent 1290 UHPLC system coupled to an Agilent 6495B QQQ mass spectrometer in positive-ion mode. A binary gradient of 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and acetonitrile (B) was used (50% to 100% B in 15 min) at a flow rate of 0.35 mL/min and 55 °C.

A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. P-values were calculated using Prism 8 (GraphPad Software). For comparisons of random distributions, the Mann-Whitney test was used, while one-way or two-way ANOVA was employed for multiple group comparisons. To examine changes between groups, the unpaired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test was utilized and Bonferroni t-tests served as post hoc tests for multiple comparisons. For correlation analyses, an alpha value < 0.05 was considered significant, and Spearman correlation (r) as well as simple linear regression (R 2 ) were calculated.

The CD4/CD8 ratios in the oral mucosa of PLWH are intact and are comparable to uninfected healthy controls (Control). 4 However, since CD4 + CD25 + FOXP3 + regulatory cells (T regs ) are increased and dysfunctional in PLWH, 4 we first determined the expression of CD25 and FOXP3 in CD8 + T cells in the gingival mucosa of PLWH ( n = 40), comparing them with uninfected healthy controls (Control) ( n = 29), by processing the tissues for multi-parameter flow cytometry ex vivo . Although ∼8–15% of CD8 + cells were FOXP3 + CD25 + , there were no significant differences between Control and PLWH groups ( Figure S1 ). To determine the CD8-T cell functionality, we evaluated the expression of IFN-γ and PD-1, the markers of effector function and hypofunctional state of CD8 T cells, respectively. 12 CD8 + T cells in PLWH had reduced percentage of IFN-γ + cells but significantly higher expression of PD-1 than the Control group ( Figures 1 A–1D). Local IFN-γ signaling in CD8 + T cells serves an important autoregulatory role by reinforcing high-avidity T cell entry into the memory pool and acquisition of T RM properties. 13 Therefore, we evaluated the percentage of CD8 + T RM cells. CXCR6 (chemokine receptor for chemokines CXCL16), CD69, CD103, and BCL-2 serve as T RM phenotypic markers and are necessary for optimal generation, survival, and facilitate entry and retention of CD8 + T RM cells in the mucosal epithelium. 2 , 10 , 14 , 15 Therefore, we determined the percentage of CD45RO + CXCR6 + ( Figures 1 E and 1F, upper panel), CD103 + CD69 + ( Figures 1 E and 1G, lower panel), and BCL-2 expression ( Figures 1 H and 1I) in the CD8 + population and found that they were significantly lower in PLWH. Also, RNA sequencing of gingival tissues, comparing PLWH with controls, revealed that some of the T cell exhaustion and apoptosis genes, such as PRDM1, SLC16A3, HIFA, NFATC2, NFAT5, NFATC1, SOCS5, BCL2A1, BCL2L11(BIM), MCL1, BID, and AIF1, were upregulated in PLWH ( Figure 1 J). However, the CD8-cytolytic program related genes like PRF1 and GZMB were unchanged. Taken together, the results not only identified T RM -like CD8 + cells in the oral mucosa for the first time, but they also showed a significant reduction in these cells in PLWH. The above findings on gingival CD8 + mucosal cells of PLWH ( Figure 1 ), and the role of polyamine dysregulation in defining mucosal CD4 + T cell fates and functions in PLWH, 5 prompted us to determine whether polyamines modulate CD8 T RM cells in vitro . We employed the oral lymphoid system of TCR-activated human tonsil organoid cultures (HTOC), where CD4 + and CD8 + T cells can be studied concurrently in cocultures. 5 We stimulated the T cells with CD3 and CD28 antibodies in the presence of TGF-β and IL-2, which induced sufficient activation, cytokine expression, and FOXP3 expression in HTOC. 5 , 9 , 16 Exogenous polyamines such as Spermidine and Putrescine hydrochloride (Putrescine), and polyamine pathway inhibitors 9 were added at the beginning of TCR stimulation of the cells. To disrupt polyamine metabolism at various stages, we employed DFMO to inhibit ornithine decarboxylase (ODC-1), a rate-limiting enzyme in the polyamine biosynthesis pathway. We also used N1-guanyl-1,7-diaminoheptane (GC7), a spermidine analog, to block EIF5A hypusination. First, we examined whether the addition of polyamines perturbed TCR induced activation by measuring the early activation marker, CD25. We found a significant CD25 upregulation upon stimulation, but neither exogenous polyamines nor polyamine pathway perturbation affected CD25 upregulation in stimulated cells ( Figure S2 ). FOXP3 expression was also not significantly affected by polyamine treatment or inhibition of the pathway ( Figure S3 ). However, exogenous polyamines significantly reduced IFN-γ expression ( Figures 2 A and 2B). Conversely, DFMO and GC7 upregulated IFN-γ in TCR-stimulated CD8 + T cells ( Figures 2 A and 2B). Also, confirming the role of hypusination, polyamines enhanced the expression of hypusinated-EIF5A, and DFMO and GC7 repressed hypusinated-EIF5A expression in CD8 + T cells ( Figures 2 C and 2D). We also found that PD-1 expression was induced with TCR stimulation and was co-expressed with IFN-γ ( Figure 2 A, y axis), indicating that PD-1 is not associated with T cell exhaustion signature in this context. As lymphoid tissues such as tonsils harbor T cells with T RM phenotype, we then examined whether polyamine pathway affected the frequency of CD8 + T RM -like cells in vitro . We found that TCR stimulation promotes and sustains T RM like cells ( Figures 3 A–3D; 1 st and 2 nd columns). Concurring with in vivo PLWH results, while exogenously added polyamines reduced the percentages of CD45RO + CXCR6 + ( Figures 3 A and 3C; 3 rd and 4 th columns) and CD103 + CD69 + ( Figures 3 B and 3D; 3 rd and 4 th columns), DFMO and GC7 treatment enhanced the percentages of these cells ( Figures 3 A–3D; 5 th and 6 th columns). Because IFN-γ is known to provide a positive feedback loop in inducing CD8 memory cells, 13 we hypothesized that induction and proliferation of these cells may require IFN-γ. To investigate the impact of IFN-γ on CD8 + T RM cell dynamics, we quantified the percentages of these cells in the presence of exogenous IFN-γ at a concentration of 20 ng/mL and an α-IFN-γ antibody at 10 μg/mL. Consistent with our hypothesis, the addition of IFN-γ significantly increased the percentages of T RM- like cells, whereas blocking IFN-γ reduced their proportions in vitro ( Figures 3 A–3D; 7th and 8th columns). Because polyamine accumulation was observed during HIV infection and T cell dysfunction, 4 , 5 we examined their effect on CD45RO + CD8 + effector memory like T cells. To mimic HIV infection followed by anti-retroviral treatment in patients ( Figure 1 ), we added the antiretroviral inhibitor efavirenz (Efa), 24–36 h after HIV infection and allowed the cells to expand with Efa for 6–7 days. Our results showed that polyamines and HIV infection did not affect CD8 + cell death. As determined by KI67 expression, they decreased the proliferation of CD45RO + CD8 + T cells ( Figure S4 ). Moreover, blockade of EIF5A hypusination restored CD45RO + CD8 + T cell proliferation ( Figure S4 ; last panel). To further determine whether polyamines or HIV-dependent EIF5A hypusination play a role in the T cell exhaustion program directly, we determined PD-1 expression along with the cytokine expression in CD8 + T cells. As we observed earlier ( Figure 2 A), polyamines and HIV infection did not upregulate PD-1 expression, but they reduced the expression of TNF-α and IL-2 ( Figure S5 ). Collectively, these findings underscore the polyamine pathway as a critical suppressor of cytokine expression, which in turn influences the proliferation of CD8 + CD45RO + T RM like cells. Moreover, the effects of HIV and polyamines on proliferation and cytokine expression appear to be independent of PD-1-driven exhaustion program or cell death in TRM-like CD8 + T cells. Resident microbial polyamines contribute significantly to the polyamine pool in the mucosal surfaces. 17 Notably, colonization by polyamine-producing bacteria is known to elevate intracellular polyamine levels in colonocytes, promoting epithelial renewal and modulating immune responses in the gut. While the PLWH oral microbiome has been studied before, findings have not been consistently replicated across different cohorts. 18 , 19 , 20 More importantly, how resident microbes relevant to polyamine metabolism are affected during chronic HIV infection is unknown. Therefore, we examined the microbial communities by performing 16S rRNA sequencing using the DNA from saliva samples collected from control ( n = 26) and PLWH ( n = 40) groups, as described in methods. 21 For bacteriome analysis, the bases at the end of the sequence with lower quality (quality score <35) were trimmed. We used DADA2 to taxonomically classify filtered reads into amplicon sequence variant (ASV) based on the SILVA database with 99% phylogenetic similarity.

We used the R package “microbiome Marker” to conduct Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) to identify microbial taxa that are statistically different between groups and to estimate the effect size of these differences using linear discriminant analysis. We used Prevalence-based and Frequency-based methods in the R package decontam to remove decontamination based on the comparison of prevalence between samples and negative controls and based on the comparison of frequency between samples and negative controls. Based on previous microbiome studies on saliva samples, 22 , 23 the healthy oral microbiome includes Streptococcus, Neisseria, Prevotella, Haemophilus, Rothia, Actinomycetaceae, Granulicatella, Corynebacterium, Actinomyces, Capnocytophaga, Porphyromonas, Veillonella, and Fusobacterium. Visualization of raw read counts showed good read depth ( Figure S6 ), and the oral microbiome diversity observed in our saliva samples was consistent with the literature ( Figure 4 A). Shannon and Chao indices defining species richness (number of species) and evenness (how evenly individuals are distributed among those species), and richness estimation demonstrated a higher bacterial diversity in PLWH compared to healthy controls ( Figure 4 B, left and right). PcoA analysis showed that the Control and PLWH groups were significantly dissimilar. ( Figure 4 C). An enrichment of 23 genera of bacteria, including Fusobacteria, Prevotella, and Megasphaera, was observed in PLWH, when compared to uninfected controls ( Figures 4 D and 4E). Among the highly enriched genera, Fusobacterium and its abundance are known to be associated with polyamine-mediated changes in host cells. 24 Since putrescine levels are known to be elevated in PLWH compared to Control, 5 we determined whether there was a correlation between Fusobacteria and putrescine levels. Human saliva samples were processed for metabolite extraction, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis. Spearman correlation analysis showed that the abundance of Fusobacteria positively correlated with salivary putrescine levels both in Control and PLWH, showing a strong link between Fusobacteria and polyamine metabolism ( Figure 4 F, top and middle). When both the groups were combined, the correlation showed more significance ( Figure 4 F, bottom). However, Prevotella and Streptococcus, two of the other putrescine-synthesizing bacteria, did not show any correlation with salivary putrescine levels ( Figure S7 ). Also, there was no correlation between Fusobacteria and the levels of Arginine, another key component of polyamine metabolism ( Figure S8 ). Thus, by revealing that Fusobacteria abundance coincides with increased putrescine levels in PLWH, these results suggest a potential interaction between dysbiosis and host polyamine metabolism. We next addressed whether polyamines are directly produced by Fusobacterium nucleatum (FN), one of the most common oral Fusobacteria species. By growing the bacteria in anaerobic conditions in the presence or absence of ornithine, we validated that they have a functional polyamine synthesis pathway. 25 , 26 We found that ornithine led to significantly greater growth than the medium without ornithine ( Figure 5 A). We also quantified putrescine, spermine, spermidine, and ornithine in cellular lysates and bacterial supernatants using targeted LC-MS analysis. 5 , 27 Intracellular concentrations of spermidine, putrescine, and ornithine were higher in FN cells cultured with ornithine ( Figure 5 B). Analysis of the spent medium revealed a substantial depletion of ornithine alongside the increase in putrescine concentration ( Figure 5 C). These findings indicate that Fusobacteria sp. effectively utilizes ornithine for growth and putrescine production. Although the oral mucosa of PLWH exhibits a higher frequency of conventional T regs and dysfunctional FOXP3 + T regs contributing to Th hyperactivation, 4 , 28 driven by polyamine dysregulation, 5 the fate of T RM cells in the context of Fusobacteria has not been evaluated. Based on polyamine effects on HTOC T cells in vitro and the ability of Fusobacteria to produce Putrescine ( Figures 2 , 3 , and 4 ), we hypothesized that reduced T RM cells may correlate with Fusobacteria abundance. In line with this tenet, we found that Fusobacteria showed a negative correlation with the frequency of CD8 + IFN-γ + cells ( Figure 6 A) and CD8 + CD45RO + CXCR6 + T RM cells ( Figure 6 B), but showed a positive correlation with CD4 + FOXP3 + T regs ( Figure 6 C), in oral gingival mucosa. However, there was no correlation between Fusobacteria and CD8 + CD69 + CD103 + cells ( Figure S9 ). These correlative results suggested that Fusobacteria could be contributing to the alterations in both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells in vivo . To determine whether Fusobacterium directly impacts CD8 + T cells in the context of HIV infection, we employed the oral lymphoid system of HIV-infected TCR-activated human tonsil organoid cultures (HTOC) in the presence of Fusobacterium lysates in vitro . 5 First, we examined PD-1 and IFN-γ expression in uninfected and infected HTOC. ( Figures 7 A and S10 ; upper panel). HIV-infection reduced IFN-γ in CD8 + cells, irrespective of upregulating PD-1 expression, but Efa partially restored the percentage of IFN-γ + cells. Most of the IFN-γ + cells are PD-1 + IFN-γ + , suggesting that PD-1-expressing cells are cytokine-expressing activated cells, and not the classical exhausted cells. FN lysate further lowered IFN-γ expression both in uninfected and HIV-infected cultures, even in the presence of Efa ( Figures 7 A and S10 ; lower panel). Although FN increased the FOXP3 expression (T regs ), ( Figure S11 ) in CD4 + T cells, HIV and FN did not change the FOXP3 expression in CD8 + T cells ( Figures 7 B and S12 ). Similar to our previous findings showed that TLR-2 ligands promoted the induction and proliferation of dysfunctional FOXP3 + T regs 4 , FN also moderately increased FOXP3 + PD-1 + IFN-γ + CD4 + cells (Dysfunctional FOXP3 + T regs ) ( Figure S13 ) and AREG expression ( Figure S14 ) in T regs in the same cultures. Consistent with our previous findings, 4 , 28 HIV triggered cell death in CD4 + T cells, including T regs , leading to decreased CD4 + FOXP3 + cells in cultures ( Figure S11 ). However, FN reduced the percentages of CD45RO + CXCR6 + ( Figures 7 C and S15 ) and CD103 + CD69 + ( Figures 7 D and S16 ) T RM cells, in the presence and absence of HIV infection. Most notably, the additive effects of HIV infection and FN resulted in a more pronounced reduction of T RM cells in cultures ( Figures 7 A–7D). While the long-term survival of T RM cells is dependent on the antiapoptotic protein BCL-2 in vivo , which exhibited reduced expression in PLWH ( Figure 1 ), neither HIV infection nor FN influenced BCL-2 expression within CD8 + T cells in vitro ( Figure S17 ). In conclusion, these findings suggest that polyamines, upregulated in CD4 + T cells during HIV infection, 4 , 5 and those derived from FN, inhibit IFN-γ in CD8 + cells, thereby reducing the proliferation and proportion of T RM cells. We next determined whether polyamine enrichment during HIV infection 5 and contributed by FN lysate ( Figure 5 ) was required for the loss of IFN-γ and TRM cells in HIV-infected HTOC treated with FN. We also examined whether the mechanism required ODC-1 activity and EIF5A hypusination in T cells. We infected HTOC T cells with HIV in the presence of FN, with and without Difluoromethylornithine (DFMO), an ODC-1 inhibitor, and GC7, a DHPS inhibitor. sections.discussion:
CD8 + tissue-resident memory (T RM ) cells are pivotal for local immune defense at mucosal barrier sites. This study elucidates the polyamine-mediated effects on CD8 + TRM cell impairment caused by dysbiosis during chronic HIV infection. Our results support the idea that HIV-associated dysbiosis, marked by increased Fusobacterium abundance, enhances bacterial putrescine production within the mucosal niche, contributing to T reg dysfunction as well as to the loss of T RM cells. Employing a multifaceted approach—integrating metabolomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and functional assays, this study has explored the role of polyamines in modulating CD8 + T cell functions. Acute HIV infection coincides with the infiltration of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells into mucosal sites, leading to epithelial cell apoptosis and mucosal barrier defects. 29 Our previous research indicated no significant changes in CD4/CD8 ratios or frequencies in the oral mucosa of cART-treated chronic HIV-positive individuals. 4 , 5 However, characterization of the CD8 + population in this study, using the same cohort reveals a reduced frequency of a subset of CD8 + T cells, i.e., . , CD8 + T RM cells in their oral mucosa compared to uninfected controls ( Figure 1 ). Consistent with prior findings that showed exhaustion in HIV-specific CD8 + T RM- like in HIV-infected individuals, 30 , 31 , 32 we also observed increased PD-1 expression, reduced IFN-γ in CD8 + T cells in PLWH in the gingival mucosa ( Figure 1 ). These data suggest that CD8 + cells found in PLWH exhibit impaired effector functions and might also contribute to the decline in T RM cells. RNA sequencing revealed partial exhaustion and apoptotic signatures in PLWH ( Figure 1 J); however, a complete CD8 + T RM -cell exhaustion signature could not be specifically assessed due to the limited size of gingival biopsy samples. Future single-cell RNA sequencing will be essential to define the precise phenotypes of individual T cell subsets within the oral mucosa.

Our study further provides deeper mechanistic insights into the role of polyamines in modulating CD8 + T cell functions within the framework of mucosal dysbiosis. Polyamines upregulated EIF5A hypusination in CD8 + T cells, leading to reduced expression of IFN-γ and key T RM signature markers ( Figures 2 and 3 ). This aligns with previous research demonstrating that these metabolites modulate the cytolytic function of CD8 + T cells and some features of memory development. 10 , 33 Our study further shows that HIV and polyamine-dependent repression of IFN-γ contribute to the proliferation suppression of CD45RO + T RM like cells ( Figures S4 , S5 , and 3 ). Because IFN-γ neutralization also led to a loss of T RM -like cells in vitro ( Figure 3 ), we propose that effector IFN-γ provides a feedforward mechanism that promotes the induction and proliferation of T RM cells, 13 which can be inhibited by excessive polyamines.

While our previous research identified polyamine metabolism as a driver of immunometabolic alterations in mucosal CD4 + cells, 4 , 5 given that resident microbiota are substantial sources of polyamines, 34 , 35 this study explored the potential impact of oral microbial dysbiosis in PLWH. Comprehensive microbiome analysis revealed dysbiosis in PLWH, with elevated Fusobacteria abundance correlating with putrescine levels ( Figure 4 ). While these data were consistent with a multivariate analysis study that showed an independent effect of HIV on oral microbiota, 36 our study futher demonstrated increased abundance of Fusobacteria in our PLWH cohort. The disparity in microbial profiles may stem from differences in sample collection methods—oral rinse versus whole saliva. 36 Our results also show that increased abundance of Fusobacteria positively correlated with putrescine levels in the same cohort in our previous study. 5 Despite observations of gingivitis or periodontitis in two participants in our PLWH cohort, Fusobacteria abundance did not correlate with these conditions ( Figure S18 ). Furthermore, the positive correlation between Fusobacteria abundance and salivary putrescine levels in the PLWH cohort, combined with Fusobacteria’ s ability to utilize ornithine and produce putrescine ( Figure 5 ), implies the contribution of Fusobacteria in polyamine dysregulation . The observed decline in T RM cells and elevated levels of T regs , correlating with increased Fusobacteria abundance in PLWH ( Figure 6 ), strongly suggest that dysbiosis, coupled with chronic infection, plays an important role in immuno-metabolic changes in the oral mucosa. Although we did not find significant CD4 + T reg increases in HIV+ FN+ Efavirenz ( Figure S11 ) cultures, FN lysate caused a significant increase in CD4 + T regs in other HTOC cultures ( Figure S11 ). Heightened cell death of T regs that also occurred during HIV infection, 4 , 5 likely confounded the FN mediated T reg increase in acutely infected HTOC treated with Efa ( Figure S11 ). In PLWH, however, the oral mucosa exhibits increased levels of CD4 T regs , 4 , 5 which positively correlate with Fusobacteria abundance ( Figure 6 C).

Our results favor the notion that the increase in CD4 + T regs is at least partially attributed to the heightened abundance of Fusobacteria in PLWH. However, based on in vitro experiments, it is unlikely that the increase in CD4 + T regs is mediated directly by polyamines ( 4 , 5 Figure S3 ). These findings suggest that chronic HIV infection in PLWH disrupts polyamine regulation directly in host CD4 + T cells, 4 , 5 as well as indirectly through dysbiosis. High Fusobacterium levels in PLWH may independently promote FOXP3 + cell induction or recruitment in the mucosa through mechanisms not yet fully understood and remain to be determined in the future. Nevertheless, our results suggest that Fusobacteria may not only elevate CD4 + T regs but also be involved in T reg dysfunction and AREG expression in CD4 + T regs ( Figures S12 and S13 ) in PLWH. Next, gingival mucosal CD8 + T cells in PLWH exhibited lower levels of BCL-2—an anti-apoptotic protein—suggesting reduced cell viability of T RM cells compared to controls in vivo ( Figures 1 H and 1I), but neither HIV nor FN exposure led to BCL-2 downregulation in CD8 + T cells in HTOC cultures ( Figure S17 ). Thus, PLWH data link CD8 + T RM loss to exhaustion and apoptotic programs ( Figure 1 J), while in vitro HIV infection points to impaired proliferation. Finally, the cytokine loss in CD8 + T RM -like cells in polyamine and HIV-infected cultures did not associate with PD-1 upregulation in vitro . Polyamines, HIV, and FN did not consistently and significantly modulate PD-1 expression across the experiments, despite their ability to downregulate cytokines ( Figures S4 , S5 , S10 , and 8 ). These data imply that PD1 expression is modulated differently in invitro activated T cells, which are significantly distinct from those in chronically activated milieu in gingival tissues of PLWH. Taken together, the results highlight certain limitations of in vitro models of acute HIV infection in accurately replicating the mucosal environment observed in chronic and treated HIV infection, especially when dysbiosis in the mucosa is also a contributing factor. Both PLWH and HTOC data, however, converge on reduced IFN-γ as a common mechanism underlying CD8 + T RM loss.

FN consistently induced diminished expression of IFN-γ and T RM -like markers without affecting the activation of CD8 + T cells both in uninfected and HIV-infected cells ( Figure 7 ). Therefore, this study underscores the vital role of polyamines in the intricate interplay between microbial composition, immunometabolic regulation, and hypofunctional states in CD8 + T cells. It also uncovers novel opportunities to regulate polyamine pathways for modulating T cell responses, thereby offering potential strategies for treating chronic inflammation and dysbiosis.
